Through observational analysis of twelve classrooms, researchers found the IWB facilitates productive dialogue when combined with teacher scaffolding, established "talk rules," and appropriate classroom participation structures. However, the technology alone is not pedagogically transformative; success requires careful integration with other classroom resources and attention to both social and cognitive dimensions of collaborative learning.

authors: Meng Yew Tee
title: Sharing and cultivating tacit knowledge in an online learning environment
summary_haiku: Online graduate business students cultivated tacit knowledge through a strategic management course using naturalistic inquiry methodology. The course combined readings, threaded discussions, and a simulation game, creating a "ba" (shared context) that encouraged socialization, externalization, combination, and internalization processes aligned with Nonaka's knowledge creation model. Students reported learning tacit dimensions impossible to acquire from textbooks alone.

authors: Sinem Siyahhan & Sasha A. Barab & Michael P. Downton
title: Using activity theory to understand intergenerational play: The case of Family Quest
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined intergenerational play between parents and children (ages 9-13) using Quest Atlantis, an educational 3D game, through activity theory analysis. Five-week observations of seven parent-child dyads revealed that successful collaborative gaming required shared intentions and expertise exchange. While outcomes varied across dyads, the research demonstrated that educational video games can facilitate meaningful family bonding and learning, particularly when designed to encourage parents and children to leverage complementary skills around personally relevant narratives.

authors: Maria Beatrice Ligorio & Giuseppe Ritella
title: The collaborative construction of chronotopes during computer-supported collaborative professional tasks
summary_haiku: # Summary This study analyzes how teachers collaboratively construct spatial and temporal frameworks during computer-supported professional planning using qualitative video analysis of six sessions. The researchers identified three distinct chronotopes—Adagio, Andante, and Allegretto—representing different interaction tempos shaped by tool features, activity complexity, and participant expertise. Results demonstrate that technology mediates collaboration by creating multiple overlapping spaces where different types of coordination emerge, revealing how space-time co-construction fundamentally influences group professional work.

authors: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse
title: CSCL in Asia
summary_haiku: Asian countries are achieving superior educational outcomes through forward-looking policies emphasizing collaborative knowledge building and twenty-first-century skills rather than rote learning. This editorial examines CSCL research and implementation across Asia, highlighting Singapore's multi-level reform approach integrating micro, meso, and macro educational scales, and presenting empirical studies on productive failure, peer review, and inquiry-based learning from Asian contexts.

authors: Chee-Kit Looi & Hyo-Jeong So & Yancy Toh & Wenli Chen
title: The Singapore experience: Synergy of national policy, classroom practice and design research
summary_haiku: Singapore's systemic approach to CSCL integration demonstrates how design research methodology bridges macro-level policy, meso-level school implementation, and micro-level classroom interactions. Through the GroupScribbles project across multiple schools, researchers co-designed collaborative learning activities with teachers, developed design principles for rapid collaborative knowledge improvement, and achieved sustainable adoption. This multi-level alignment of policy, practice, and research provides a model for scaling CSCL innovations while addressing real classroom constraints.

authors: Manu Kapur
title: Temporality matters: Advancing a method for analyzing problem-solving processes in a computer-supported collaborative environment
summary_haiku: This study advances Lag-sequential Analysis (LsA) as a quantitative method for examining temporal patterns in computer-supported collaborative learning groups. Applied to synchronous online problem-solving discussions, LsA revealed significant sequential interaction patterns invisible to traditional "coding and counting" approaches. Critically, temporal transition patterns between process categories emerged as the strongest predictor of group performance, demonstrating that analyzing the order and sequence of collaborative interactions—not merely their frequency—is essential for understanding collaborative learning processes.

authors: Suneeta A. Pathak & Beaumie Kim & Michael J. Jacobson & Baohui Zhang
title: Learning the physics of electricity: A qualitative analysis of collaborative processes involved in productive failure
summary_haiku: This qualitative study examines collaborative problem-solving dynamics in physics education using computer-supported learning. Two student dyads—one experiencing productive failure through initial low-structured activities followed by high-structured ones, and another receiving only high-structured activities—solved electricity problems using NetLogo models. Analysis of video, screen captures, and solutions revealed that initial struggle enabled deeper engagement with the model and reflective reasoning, while over-scripted activities hindered meaningful collaboration and conceptual understanding.

authors: Zi-gang Ge
title: Exploring e-learners’ perceptions of net-based peer-reviewed English writing
summary_haiku: This study examined asynchronous, blind peer review for improving Chinese adult e-learners' English writing. Thirty-six students divided into three ability groups participated in a year-long experiment with rotating cross-group peer reviews mediated by the instructor. Results showed all groups improved, with lower-ability students making greater progress than higher-ability students. However, high-ability students became discouraged when paired with lower-ability peers for extended periods, suggesting flexible grouping strategies may be necessary.

authors: Michael Glassman & Min Ju Kang
title: The logic of wikis: The possibilities of the Web 2.0 classroom
summary_haiku: Web 2.0 tools like wikis and blogs can enable Dewey's vision of democratic education by supporting abductive reasoning—the logic of hypothesis generation essential for creative problem-solving. Unlike traditional deductive approaches emphasizing certainty, abduction requires simultaneously maintaining multiple competing premises, a capability previously impossible in classrooms but now feasible through hypertext-based technologies that create scale-free networks of interconnected information nodes.

authors: Baruch B. Schwarz & Yaron Schur & Haim Pensso & Naama Tayer
title: Perspective taking and synchronous argumentation for learning the day/night cycle
summary_haiku: Combining perspective-taking through pictures and synchronous computer-supported argumentation promotes conceptual learning of the day/night cycle in Grade 8 students. Using the Digalo tool and design-research methodology with pre-post testing, the study found significant improvements in mental models, elaboration, and knowledge integration. However, teacher mediation during small-group discussions did not enhance learning outcomes, suggesting that meticulous task design and peer argumentation were primary drivers of conceptual change.

authors: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse
title: Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend
summary_haiku: This editorial argues that the CSCL field benefits from diverse theoretical, methodological, and pedagogical approaches rather than convergence on single paradigms. The authors advocate for pluralism in research perspectives, illustrating how multiple schools of thought—from dialogical to information-processing frameworks—advance understanding of collaborative learning. They present diverse studies examining practice, theory, analysis methods, and technology design, demonstrating that CSCL's complexity requires multifaceted inquiry.

authors: Carol K. K. Chan
title: Bridging research and practice: Implementing and sustaining knowledge building in Hong Kong classrooms
summary_haiku: # Summary This article examines how computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) research translates into classroom practice through a case study of knowledge-building implementation in Hong Kong schools. Using design-based research across macro (policy), meso (teacher networks), and micro (classroom) levels, the study identifies three critical themes: systemic alignment across educational levels, capacity building through principle-based teacher communities, and innovation as continuous inquiry. Findings demonstrate that sustained CSCL adoption requires coordinating institutional policies, teacher professional development networks, and classroom design while adapting research models to local socio-cultural contexts.

authors: Manoli Pifarre & Judith Kleine Staarman
title: Wiki-supported collaborative learning in primary education: How a dialogic space is created for thinking together
summary_haiku: This study examined how wikis support primary students' collaborative knowledge construction through a dialogic lens. Twenty-five students engaged in a science project using MediaWiki, combining asynchronous wiki interaction with synchronous face-to-face collaboration. Analysis revealed students developed exploratory, cumulative, and disputational talk patterns, establishing intersubjective understanding. The collaborative wiki text demonstrated greater complexity, length, and reasoning than initial individual proposals, supporting the claim that dialogic approaches enhance wiki-based collaborative learning.

authors: Robert L. Jorczak
title: An information processing perspective on divergence and convergence in collaborative learning
summary_haiku: Jorczak proposes a Collaborative Information Processing (CIP) model explaining how peer discussion facilitates learning through information divergence and convergence. Using information processing theory, the model demonstrates that groups benefit from diverse member perspectives triggering conceptual conflict, followed by convergent processes achieving shared understanding. The CIP framework unifies cognitive and social interaction theories, predicting that heterogeneous groups and divergent information exchange enhance collaborative learning outcomes.

authors: Bas Kolloffel & Tessa H. S. Eysink & Ton de Jong
title: Comparing the effects of representational tools in collaborative and individual inquiry learning
summary_haiku: Collaborative learners significantly outperformed individual learners in combinatorics and probability inquiry learning, particularly on intuitive and situational knowledge. Using a pre-test/post-test design with 61 collaborative dyads and 95 individual students, three representational tool formats (conceptual, arithmetical, textual) were compared. Results showed collaboration's benefits persisted regardless of tool use, while individual learners benefited from externalization. Representational format did not directly enhance specific knowledge types as hypothesized, though approximately 50% adopted conceptual or textual tools versus only 20% using arithmetical formats.

authors: Michael A. Evans & Eliot Feenstra & Emily Ryon & David McNeill
title: A multimodal approach to coding discourse: Collaboration, distributed cognition, and geometric reasoning
summary_haiku: Researchers developed a multimodal coding framework to analyze distributed cognition in young children's collaborative problem-solving. Using speech, gesture, and gaze analysis, they tracked "coreferences"—shared references to objects, participants, and concepts—across three discourse levels. Applied to 7-8-year-olds solving tangrams physically and virtually, findings revealed increased meta-level communication and coalition formation in computer-supported settings, with dominant participants showing greater influence in virtual versus physical environments.

authors: Erin Walker & Nikol Rummel & Kenneth R. Koedinger
title: Designing automated adaptive support to improve student helping behaviors in a peer tutoring activity
summary_haiku: Researchers used a four-phase iterative design process to develop adaptive support for peer tutoring in algebra. Through user needs analysis, system design, classroom experimentation, and qualitative case analysis, they found that adaptive assistance improved conceptual help quality and sentence classifier usage compared to fixed support, though learning gains were not significantly different. The study demonstrates how accountability-focused design principles can enhance collaborative help-giving behaviors.

authors: Ulrike Cress & Katrin Wodzicki & Martina Bientzle & Andreas Lingnau
title: CSCL for intellectually disabled pupils: Stimulating interaction by using a floor control mechanism
summary_haiku: This study examined whether floor control mechanisms—restricting simultaneous actions in collaborative learning environments—improve interaction quality for intellectually disabled pupils. Twenty pupils completed a furniture-sorting task in pairs using tablet PCs, comparing floor control versus unrestricted conditions. Results showed floor control reduced relocations, decreased coordinative communication, and increased content-related discussion, particularly when pupils disagreed or faced difficult symbols, while producing slightly higher-quality collaborative outcomes.

authors: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse
title: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich W. Hesse & Nancy Law
summary_haiku: # Summary The CSCL 2011 conference in Hong Kong demonstrated significant growth in computer-supported collaborative learning research, particularly in Asia-Pacific regions, with over 400 participants from 30+ countries. The conference emphasized connecting CSCL research to educational policy and practice through keynotes, workshops, and post-conference events across Chinese cities, establishing CSCL as a vital research field globally.

authors: Cliff Lampe & Donghee Yvette Wohn & Jessica Vitak & Nicole B. Ellison & Rick Wash
title: Student use of Facebook for organizing collaborative classroom activities
summary_haiku: Two survey studies examined how undergraduate students repurpose Facebook for classroom organizing. Study 1 (N=302) found that Facebook intensity and willingness to contact instructors predicted collaboration propensity. Study 2 (N=214) revealed two distinct collaboration types: positive (instructor-approved) and negative (unapproved), with different predictors including self-efficacy and relational communication strategies, suggesting how students use Facebook matters more than frequency.

authors: Fengfeng Ke & Alicia F. Chavez & Pei-Ni L. Causarano & Antonio Causarano
title: Identity presence and knowledge building: Joint emergence in online learning environments?
summary_haiku: This mixed-method study examined identity presence in seven online courses and its relationship to knowledge building. Using discourse analysis of 1,817 discussion posts, researchers found that posts expressing personal experiences, cultural perspectives, and age-related views elicited significantly more responses and correlated with knowledge-sharing interactions. However, identity presence did not significantly predict higher-level collaborative knowledge construction, suggesting online learners prioritize self-expression over negotiating shared understanding.

authors: Hao-Chuan Wang & Carolyn P. Rose & Chun-Yen Chang
title: Agent-based dynamic support for learning from collaborative brainstorming in scientific inquiry
summary_haiku: This study examines learning during collaborative brainstorming through two controlled experiments manipulating individual versus pair work and system support. Results reveal that while pair brainstorming produces process losses in idea generation, it enhances multi-perspective learning. The VIBRANT agent's automatic feedback improves connection-based learning. An enhanced version in study two shows promise for mitigating productivity losses associated with collaborative work.

authors: Shiou-Wen Yeh & Jia-Jiunn Lo & Jeng-Jia Huang
title: Scaffolding collaborative technical writing with procedural facilitation and synchronous discussion
summary_haiku: Researchers developed Process-Writing Wizard, a computer-supported system combining procedural scaffolding and synchronous chat to facilitate collaborative technical writing among EFL students. An experimental study with 48 students compared the system against standard chat. Results showed experimental group students demonstrated significantly higher perceived usefulness, positive attitudes, and stronger intention to reuse the system. Their articles exhibited superior content and organization quality, and synchronous discussions focused more on article-related interactions rather than social exchanges.

authors: Dejana Mullins & Nikol Rummel & Hans Spada
title: Are two heads always better than one? Differential effects of collaboration on students’ computer-supported learning in mathematics
summary_haiku: Collaboration's effectiveness in mathematics learning depends on instructional material type. This experimental study compared individual versus collaborative learning with conceptual and procedural algebra instruction in a computer-supported environment. Results showed collaboration enhanced conceptual knowledge acquisition through mutual elaboration, but hindered procedural skill development due to task distribution and reduced practice opportunities.

authors: Alyssa Friend Wise
title: Analyzing temporal patterns of knowledge construction in a role-based online discussion
summary_haiku: This study analyzed temporal patterns of knowledge construction in role-based online discussions using content analysis and statistical discourse analysis. Examining 252 posts from 21 university students, researchers identified pivotal posts that divided discussions into distinct segments. Results showed most discussions progressed from lower to higher knowledge construction phases, with mid-discussion summaries by Synthesizer and Wrapper roles acting as pivotal posts that elevated subsequent discussion quality, supporting the progressive nature of collaborative knowledge construction.

authors: Francesca Pozzi
title: The impact of scripted roles on online collaborative learning processes
summary_haiku: This pilot study examined how scripted "opinion-centered" roles impact online collaborative learning in an asynchronous text-based environment. Using content analysis of 209 student messages and post-activity questionnaires, researchers evaluated four dimensions: participative, social, cognitive, and teaching. Results showed roles effectively fostered group cohesion and knowledge building, though metacognition remained underdeveloped. Students' perceptions largely aligned with message analysis, indicating awareness of the collaborative process.

authors: Gerry Stahl
title: Collaborating around the tabletop
summary_haiku: Tabletop computing environments can serve as focal points for collaborative learning by integrating physical and digital artifacts, spoken and written texts, and computational support. This editorial introduces a flash theme examining how tabletop interfaces support small-group interaction, exploring design considerations, interaction patterns, scripted collaboration, and community building across diverse educational contexts.

authors: Pierre Dillenbourg
title: Interactive tabletops in education
summary_haiku: Interactive tabletops support co-located collaborative learning through hands-on manipulation of objects, conveying socio-constructivist pedagogical approaches. This analytical framework examines 33 design considerations across four levels: user-system interaction, teamwork dynamics, classroom orchestration, and socio-cultural contexts. The authors argue that tabletops' educational effectiveness depends on thoughtful design addressing these specific affordances rather than inherent technological properties.

authors: Steven E. Higgins & Emma Mercier & Elizabeth Burd & Andrew Hatch
title: Multi-touch tables and the relationship with collaborative classroom pedagogies: A synthetic review
summary_haiku: Multi-touch tables offer significant potential for supporting collaborative classroom learning through their design features. This synthetic review proposes a typology categorizing hardware characteristics—surface geometry and display type, touch sensing capabilities, and connectivity—to analyze how technical affordances align with pedagogical goals. Evidence suggests horizontal multi-touch surfaces enable more equitable participation and task-focused interaction than traditional single-touch technologies, though text entry limitations and teacher orchestration challenges require further investigation.

authors: Taciana Pontual Falcao & Sara Price
title: Interfering and resolving: How tabletop interaction facilitates co-construction of argumentative knowledge
summary_haiku: Peer interference in shared tabletop interfaces can productively support argumentative knowledge co-construction during exploratory science learning. Analyzing 43 students aged 11-14 interacting with a tangible light-behavior simulation, researchers applied Weinberger and Fischer's consensus-building framework to interference episodes. Integration-oriented consensus building—where students reflected on and incorporated peers' contributions—consistently produced productive learning, while conflict-oriented approaches typically yielded counter-productive outcomes.

authors: Eyal Szewkis & Miguel Nussbaum & Tal Rosen & Jose Abalos & Fernanda Denardin & Daniela Caballero & Arturo Tagle & Cristian Alcoholado
title: Collaboration within large groups in the classroom
summary_haiku: This study investigates large-group classroom collaboration using Single Display Groupware with multiple mice and minimal hardware. Through an experimental design comparing 42 students using the system for 40% of class time against 32 control students, researchers found that "silent collaboration"—a negotiation mechanism enabling object exchanges—effectively facilitated synchronous learning in Spanish language tasks. Results demonstrated significant learning gains and successful achievement of collaborative conditions, suggesting this low-cost approach enables effective large-group computer-supported collaborative learning.

authors: Giulia Gelmini-Hornsby & Shaaron Ainsworth
title: Guided reciprocal questioning to support children’s collaborative storytelling
summary_haiku: Guided Reciprocal Peer Questioning (GRPQ) scripts significantly enhance children's collaborative storytelling through increased interactive discussion. Using a within-subjects design with 36 six-to-seven-year-olds creating stories with KidPad, the study found that question prompts promoted longer, more evaluatively rich, and more coherent stories. Benefits largely persisted after scaffold withdrawal, suggesting children internalized the questioning approach and can apply it independently.

authors: Inge Molenaar & Ming Ming Chiu & Peter Sleegers & Carla van Boxtel
title: Scaffolding of small groups’ metacognitive activities with an avatar
summary_haiku: Avatar-based metacognitive scaffolding in small group learning environments influences student knowledge acquisition through mediation by metacognitive activities. Multivariate multilevel analysis of 51,339 conversation turns from 54 elementary students revealed that problematizing scaffolds (eliciting student explanations) produced greater domain knowledge than structuring scaffolds (providing examples), with metacognitive activities mediating these effects. Both scaffold types enhanced metacognitive knowledge primarily through increased metacognitive engagement.

authors: Donatella Cesareni & Francesca Martini & Ilaria Mancini
title: Building a community among teachers, researchers and university students. A blended approach to training
summary_haiku: # Summary This case study examined a blended learning community of 45 Italian teachers, researchers, and university students participating in the ITCOLE project. Using qualitative analysis of face-to-face and online interactions, researchers found that expert teachers assumed central roles while novice teachers engaged in legitimate peripheral participation, gradually becoming more competent community members. Teachers recognized CSCL's innovative potential for student motivation and collaborative knowledge building, though they identified challenges including technical infrastructure limitations and heavy workload demands.

authors: Gerry Stahl
title: Ethnomethodologically informed
summary_haiku: Ethnomethodology (EM), founded by Harold Garfinkel, offers a research approach particularly suited to analyzing computer-supported collaborative learning by examining how people create intersubjective understanding through observable meaning-making methods. Unlike traditional educational research emphasizing individual mental states or societal forces, EM focuses on small-group interactions through sequential discourse analysis, enabling researchers to understand collaborative learning processes without imposing predetermined theoretical frameworks.

authors: Christian Greiffenhagen
title: Making rounds: The routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers
summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological study analyzes teacher interventions during collaborative computer-based learning using video recordings of English lessons with storyboarding software. Through detailed conversation analysis of naturally occurring classroom interactions, the author identifies five types of teacher practices: ratifying pupil work, reminding pupils of task requirements, making suggestions for improvement, maintaining classroom control, and making whole-class announcements. The analysis reveals that classroom management and pedagogy are intertwined rather than separate, and tensions between teacher and pupil perspectives are collaborative rather than antagonistic.

authors: Ulrika Bennerstedt & Jonas Ivarsson & Jonas Linderoth
title: How gamers manage aggression: Situating skills in collaborative computer games
summary_haiku: Using ethnomethodological analysis of boss encounters in a massively multiplayer online game, this study examines skills gamers develop during collaborative gameplay involving portrayed aggression. The researchers found that "aggression" and "collaboration" manifest as highly specialized, game-specific practices—particularly aggro management—rather than transferable general skills. The analysis challenges assumptions underlying both positive and negative gaming effects research, arguing that claims about behavioral transfer require explicit theoretical justification and risk oversimplification.

authors: Kenneth Silseth
title: The multivoicedness of game play: Exploring the unfolding of a student’s learning trajectory in a gaming context at school
summary_haiku: This qualitative case study examines how classroom interactions facilitate a student's learning trajectory while playing the educational game Global Conflicts: Palestine. Using sociocultural and dialogic analysis of video-recorded gameplay and discussions, the research demonstrates that computer games become learning resources through collaborative meaning-making. The teacher's role in orchestrating dialogic spaces where multiple perspectives "inter-animate" each other proved crucial for developing nuanced understanding of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict's complexity.

authors: Maarit Arvaja
title: Personal and shared experiences as resources for meaning making in a philosophy of science course
summary_haiku: Health education students in an online philosophy of science course used personal work experiences and peer contributions as meaning-making resources. Analysis of individual writings and discussions revealed three epistemic activities: applying theoretical concepts to practice, forming conceptions, and critiquing. Peer interactions involved elaboration and sharing discourse. Results demonstrate that connecting abstract philosophical knowledge to lived experience enhanced understanding while fostering boundary crossing between institutional and personal knowledge contexts.

authors: Sarah Pollack & Yifat Ben-David Kolikant
title: Collaboration amidst disagreement and moral judgment: The dynamics of Jewish and Arab students’ collaborative inquiry of their joint past
summary_haiku: Israeli Jewish and Arab students collaboratively investigated a historical event through computer-supported learning, analyzing conflicting narratives via wiki-based discussion. Despite persistent disagreement, students' post-activity individual answers demonstrated enriched historical understanding, incorporating multiple perspectives and reduced one-sidedness. The researchers propose "fission"—moments when opposing voices create cracks in individual perspectives, fostering polyphonic thinking without requiring consensus.

authors: Yangjie Song & Chee-Kit Looi
title: Linking teacher beliefs, practices and student inquiry-based learning in a CSCL environment: A tale of two teachers
summary_haiku: Teachers holding innovation-oriented beliefs about inquiry-based learning enacted mathematics lessons with inquiry principle-based practices and technology-enhanced orchestration, while teachers with teacher-centered beliefs used traditional approaches. Comparative case analysis of two teachers using Group Scribbles technology revealed that innovation-oriented beliefs directly shaped progressive inquiry practices, which subsequently fostered student collaborative knowledge construction and effective technology use.

authors: Javier Onrubia & Anna Engel
title: The role of teacher assistance on the effects of a macro-script in collaborative writing tasks
summary_haiku: This multiple-case study examines how teacher assistance patterns interact with macro-scripts to influence collaborative writing in university students. Analyzing two settings with different script types and teaching approaches, the study identifies distinct teacher assistance patterns and their relationships to group organization and knowledge construction phases. Results show that flexible, content-focused teacher guidance combined with open scripts promotes heterogeneous group strategies and advanced collaborative knowledge construction, while detailed scripts paired with organizational reminders produce homogeneous adherence but lower knowledge construction levels.

authors: Gerry Stahl
title: Cognizing mediating: Unpacking the entanglement of artifacts with collective minds
summary_haiku: Human cognition and technological artifacts mutually shape each other through dialectical processes. This editorial examines instrumental genesis theory—how artifacts evolve through use—comparing it with affordances and structuration theories. The analysis emphasizes that CSCL research should focus on small-group collective cognition, design complex collaborative tasks beyond individual capability, and employ multiple methodologies to understand how groups enact technological mediation during knowledge building.

authors: Maarten Overdijk & Wouter van Diggelen & Paul A. Kirschner & Michael Baker
title: Connecting agents and artifacts in CSCL: Towards a rationale of mutual shaping
summary_haiku: This article examines how human agents and technical artifacts connect in computer-supported collaborative learning. Through theoretical review of affordance, structuration, and instrumental genesis frameworks, the authors argue that existing CSCL research emphasizing artifact-driven "shaping" of collaboration should shift toward "mutual shaping," where both learners and technologies reciprocally influence each other. Instrumental genesis emerges as the most viable theoretical approach for understanding this bidirectional relationship.

authors: Jacques Lonchamp
title: An instrumental perspective on CSCL systems
summary_haiku: Rabardel's instrumental genesis theory reveals that CSCL systems involve complex two-phase development: teachers customize artifacts during preparation, while learners and tutors collaboratively develop utilization schemes during use. The research distinguishes two system categories based on who drives instrumentalization—learner-instrumentalizable systems supporting emergent collaborative practices, and teacher-instrumentalizable systems enforcing predefined learning structures—each mediating different forms of knowledge construction through epistemic, pragmatic, interpersonal, and reflexive mediation.

authors: Giuseppe Ritella & Kai Hakkarainen
title: Instrumental genesis in technology-mediated learning: From double stimulation to expansive knowledge practices
summary_haiku: Technology-mediated collaborative learning requires transforming social practices through instrumental genesis—the developmental process of appropriating technological tools as learning instruments. Drawing on sociocultural theory, the authors argue that epistemic mediation through external artifacts enables knowledge creation, but productive integration demands extended iterative efforts reformatting cognitive-cultural operating systems at personal and collective levels, explaining why innovative CSCL practices remain difficult to implement in educational systems.

authors: Carmen Zahn & Karsten Krauskopf & Friedrich W. Hesse & Roy Pea
title: How to improve collaborative learning with video tools in the classroom? Social vs. cognitive guidance for student teams
summary_haiku: Social interaction-related guidance proved more effective than cognitive task-related guidance for student teams using video tools in collaborative history learning. In a 2×2 experimental design with 148 sixteen-year-old students, teams receiving guidance emphasizing communication norms and cooperation demonstrated superior learning outcomes in historical skills and design product quality, regardless of video tool type. Results suggest focusing instructional support on group dynamics rather than task procedures.

authors: Jin Mu & Karsten Stegmann & Elijah Mayfield & Carolyn Rose & Frank Fischer
title: The ACODEA framework: Developing segmentation and classification schemes for fully automatic analysis of online discussions
summary_haiku: The ACODEA framework enables fully automatic analysis of online discussions by extracting syntactic and semantic features through part-of-speech tagging and named-entity recognition before segmentation and classification. Applied to 84 students' collaborative discussions about attribution theory, the three-layer approach achieved high reliability (Cohen's Kappa ≥0.81) for micro-argumentation coding across different contexts, demonstrating that context-independent automated analysis is feasible for collaborative learning environments.

authors: Nikol Rummel & Dejana Mullins & Hans Spada
title: Scripted collaborative learning with the cognitive tutor algebra
summary_haiku: Researchers extended the Cognitive Tutor Algebra system to support collaborative learning by implementing a jigsaw-based collaboration script with adaptive elements. In a classroom experiment comparing scripted collaboration, unscripted collaboration, and individual learning, process analyses revealed the script improved interaction quality and problem-solving during learning. However, quantitative between-condition comparisons showed no significant learning advantage for collaboration, though collaborative performance matched individual performance despite fewer practice problems, suggesting interaction compensated for reduced practice opportunities.

authors: Gerry Stahl & Nancy Law & Friedrich Hesse
title: An international research community
summary_haiku: The International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning demonstrates significant scholarly impact, ranking eleventh among education journals with a 2.243 impact factor. The journal supports a thriving international research community across fifty-three countries, publishing diverse, interdisciplinary research on collaborative learning technologies through rigorous peer review and design-based methodologies that advance CSCL theory and practice globally.

authors: Noel Enyedy & Joshua A. Danish & Girlie Delacruz & Melissa Kumar
title: Learning physics through play in an augmented reality environment
summary_haiku: # Summary This study demonstrates that first and second graders (n=43) can meaningfully learn Newtonian physics through augmented reality activities combining embodied play and progressive symbolization. Using pre-post assessments, students showed significant gains in understanding force, net force, friction, and two-dimensional motion. Two design principles guided the curriculum: participatory modeling leveraging socio-dramatic play to make intuitions visible, and progressive symbolization enabling students to invent and refine representational systems. Case studies illustrate how embodied prediction and collaborative symbol refinement supported conceptual integration, though challenges emerged when students relied exclusively on embodiment or formal reasoning.

authors: Kim MacKinnon
title: Context matters: The value of analyzing human factors within educational contexts as a way of informing technology-related decisions within design research
summary_haiku: Design research in educational technology often overlooks systematic analysis of contextual factors. This study adapts Cognitive Work Analysis (CWA), an engineering method, to systematically identify human factors constraints—political, organizational, team, psychological, and physical—within a teacher education program. Through interviews, documentation analysis, and observations, 358 constraints were identified. The modified CWA approach made contextual information explicit and organized, enabling informed technology design decisions for supporting student research projects through an online mentorship environment.

authors: Eun Mee Lim
title: Patterns of kindergarten children’s social interaction with peers in the computer area
summary_haiku: This qualitative study examined kindergarten children's peer interactions in a classroom computer area through three-month observations and teacher interviews. The researcher identified six social interaction patterns: parallel play, verbal conflicts, sociable interactions, knowledge construction through positive processes, knowledge construction through negative processes, and non-verbal communication. Three patterns—positive processes, negative processes, and non-verbal communication—constituted "Cognitively Effective Social Interaction" leading to meaningful knowledge construction. Findings demonstrate computers support collaborative learning when integrated with classroom curriculum.

authors: Mingzhu Qiu & Jim Hewitt
title: Online class size, note reading, note writing and collaborative discourse
summary_haiku: This mixed-methods study examined 25 online graduate courses (341 students, 25 instructors) using tracking logs and interviews to investigate how class size affects note reading and writing loads. Findings revealed class size positively correlates with total notes read but negatively with percentage read, indicating information overload in larger classes. Students wrote shorter, simpler notes in larger classes. Dividing large classes into subgroups reduced overload. An optimal class size of 13-15 students was identified for effective collaborative discourse.

authors: Mar Perez-Sanagustin & Patricia Santos & Davinia Hernandez-Leo & Josep Blat
title: 4SPPIces: A case study of factors in a scripted collaborative-learning blended course across spatial locations
summary_haiku: This case study evaluates the 4SPPIces model—a conceptual framework combining Space, Pedagogical Method, Participants, and History factors—for designing computer-supported collaborative blended learning scripts. Researchers implemented a geography fieldwork activity with 34 students across Barcelona using mobile devices and GPS. Results demonstrate that considering 4SPPIces factors successfully enhanced the activity, promoting collaborative skills, motivation, and learning about multiple urban districts while effectively supporting teacher orchestration through integrated technologies.

authors: Gerry Stahl
title: Traversing planes of learning
summary_haiku: CSCL research typically analyzes learning at three interconnected but separately studied levels: individual, small-group, and community. This article argues that understanding how these planes interpenetrate requires examining artifacts and resources that mediate across levels. Using bridge metaphors and phenomenological theory, Stahl proposes that collaborative knowledge-building involves sequential interaction drawing resources from all planes, with designed artifacts and language serving as key connectors enabling traversal between learning levels.

authors: Jacques Lonchamp
title: Computational analysis and mapping of ijCSCL content
summary_haiku: This empirical study employs co-word analysis to map content in the International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2006-2011). Using hierarchical clustering and multidimensional scaling on full-text corpora, the research identifies three major thematic categories: interaction analysis, technical/organizational issues, and applications. Key findings include dominant themes like scripting, monitoring, community-based learning, and argumentation, revealing the intellectual structure of CSCL research.

authors: Markus Nivala & Hans Rystedt & Roger Saljo & Pauliina Kronqvist & Erno Lehtinen
title: Interactive visual tools as triggers of collaborative reasoning in entry-level pathology
summary_haiku: Virtual microscopy enables collaborative pathology learning through multimodal referential practices. This qualitative video analysis of 15 medical student pairs examined how interactive visual tools mediate diagnostic reasoning. Students organized shared visual fields using gestures, zooming, and paced negotiations to construct joint understanding. Key strategies included framing diagnostic processes, negotiating visual evidence, and extending reasoning frames when uncertain. The study demonstrates that technology becomes constitutive of face-to-face collaboration, and understanding image production techniques proves integral to medical interpretation.

authors: Susan A. Yoon & Karen Elinich & Joyce Wang & Christopher Steinmeier & Sean Tucker
title: Using augmented reality and knowledge-building scaffolds to improve learning in a science museum
summary_haiku: A quasi-experimental study examined how augmented reality and knowledge-building scaffolds enhance science learning in a museum setting. Using four conditions with varying levels of digital augmentation and pedagogical support, researchers tested 119 middle-grade students on electrical conductivity concepts. Results showed digital augmentation alone improved conceptual knowledge, while knowledge-building scaffolds combined with augmented reality significantly enhanced students' ability to theorize about scientific phenomena, suggesting collaborative supports amplify technology-based informal learning.

authors: Chia-Ching Lin & Chin-Chung Tsai
title: Participatory learning through behavioral and cognitive engagements in an online collective information searching activity
summary_haiku: This study investigated how college students' behavioral and cognitive engagements relate during online collective information searching using social bookmarking. Through cluster analysis of 101 engineering students' activity logs and annotations, researchers identified four behavioral patterns (Hitchhiker, Individualist, Active, Commentator) and two cognitive levels (Deep, Surface). Results revealed that students exhibiting "Active" behavioral engagement demonstrated "Deep" cognitive engagement, while those with "Hitchhiker" or "Individualist" patterns showed "Surface" engagement, with deeper engagement correlating to better assignment performance.

authors: Pericles Sobreira & Pierre Tchounikine
title: A model for flexibly editing CSCL scripts
summary_haiku: Researchers developed the T2 model, a table-tree representation system enabling teachers to flexibly edit CSCL scripts. Using intuitive table structures mapped to machine-readable trees, the approach prioritizes simplicity and adaptability over complex meta-models. Usability testing with five teachers confirmed the model's ease of use and demonstrated that teachers effectively leveraged representation flexibility to customize scripts according to their perspectives and contexts.

authors: Diler Oner
title: Analyzing group coordination when solving geometry problems with dynamic geometry software
summary_haiku: This study proposes a methodological framework for analyzing group coordination in geometry problem-solving with dynamic geometry software. Using conversation analysis and reference field theory, the researcher examined a dyad's face-to-face interaction solving a construction problem. Findings reveal successful collaboration requires coordinating both mathematical/tool-enabled resources and collaborative resources, with participants shifting between theoretical and spatio-graphical reference fields while maintaining productive turn-taking and transactive dialogue.

authors: Gerry Stahl
title: Learning across levels
summary_haiku: CSCL research must bridge individual, small-group, and community levels of analysis through emergent interactional resources. This theoretical framework proposes that resources—from ephemeral conversational moves to institutionalized practices—mediate across levels through processes of reification, sedimentation, and personalization. Empirical studies examining mathematical problem-solving, scientific representations, and collaborative learning demonstrate how tracking these resources reveals connections between local interactions and broader socio-cultural contexts.

authors: Magnus Hontvedt & Hans Christian Arnseth
title: On the bridge to learn: Analysing the social organization of nautical instruction in a ship simulator
summary_haiku: This qualitative study examines how nautical students collaboratively construct simulated learning contexts through role-play in a ship simulator. Using interaction analysis of video data, the researchers identify two competing activity contexts: students enacting professional crew roles and students participating in educational training. The analysis reveals that while role-play enables situated learning opportunities for professional tasks, maintaining credible simulations requires substantial interactional effort and can conflict with instructional objectives like meta-reflection and debriefing.

authors: Anniken Furberg & Anders Kluge & Sten Ludvigsen
title: Student sensemaking with science diagrams in a computer-based setting
summary_haiku: This study examined how upper secondary students collaboratively made sense of solar panel diagrams in a computer-based learning environment. Using interaction analysis of one student group's expert-group session, researchers found that science diagrams functioned as productive social and cognitive resources, enabling students to slow conceptual reasoning and negotiate scientific meanings. However, students faced significant challenges translating oral accounts into written explanations and coordinating multiple diagram representations. The analysis reveals that students' sensemaking involved not only conceptual understanding but also navigating institutional norms and practices embedded within schooling contexts.

authors: Alan Zemel & Timothy Koschmann
title: Recalibrating reference within a dual-space interaction environment
summary_haiku: # Summary Middle school students collaborating in the Virtual Math Teams system develop shared understanding of mathematical problems through sequential recalibration of referential practices. Using ethnomethodological analysis of chat and whiteboard interactions, the study demonstrates how students progressively specify indexical properties of underspecified problems and solutions. Rather than treating representations as static objects, the research reveals how problem-solving emerges from the situated, interactive work of producing and refining references to mathematical concepts across dual-space modalities.

authors: Evren Eryilmaz & Jakko van der Pol & Terry Ryan & Philip Martin Clark & Justin Mary
title: Enhancing student knowledge acquisition from online learning conversations
summary_haiku: This experimental study compared linked and parallel artifact-centered discussion systems with 106 pharmacy students. Annotation functionality in the linked system decreased coordination activities while increasing assertion and conflict knowledge construction activities. Mediation analysis revealed that assertion, conflict, and clarification activities significantly predicted individual learning gains, with the treatment group achieving greater post-test improvements than controls.

authors: Gerry Stahl
title: Transactive discourse in CSCL
summary_haiku: This editorial examines transactivity in computer-supported collaborative learning, analyzing how students build on each other's reasoning through shared digital media. Stahl distinguishes between individual-level analysis focusing on mental states and group-level analysis examining discourse meaning. Four empirical studies explore transactivity across contexts—student blogging, scripted dyadic interactions, kindergarten collaborative computer use, and automated speech analysis—demonstrating diverse methodological approaches to measuring and supporting collaborative knowledge building.

authors: Richard Alterman & Johann Ari Larusson
title: Participation and common knowledge in a case study of student blogging
summary_haiku: This case study examines how student blogging facilitates common knowledge emergence in a loosely coordinated learning environment. Through qualitative and quantitative analysis of 25 undergraduates' semester-long blogging activity in an Internet & Society course, researchers found that common knowledge develops through distributed participation across multiple conversations and topics. Longer conversations served as focal points attracting wider readership and participation, while persistent content enabled students to mine the blogosphere when preparing papers, with approximately 50% of paper topics foreshadowed by blogging activity.

authors: Omid Noroozi & Stephanie D. Teasley & Harm J. A. Biemans & Armin Weinberger & Martin Mulder
title: Facilitating learning in multidisciplinary groups with transactive CSCL scripts
summary_haiku: # Summary This laboratory experiment with 120 university students examined how transactive memory and discussion scripts in computer-supported collaborative learning environments facilitate knowledge sharing in multidisciplinary groups. Students from different disciplinary backgrounds solved an authentic problem requiring complementary expertise. Results showed that each script individually improved transactive knowledge sharing, knowledge transfer, and solution quality, but combining both scripts produced negative interaction effects, likely due to over-scripting constraints within the 80-minute collaboration period.

authors: Florencia Gomez & Miguel Nussbaum & Juan F. Weitz & Ximena Lopez & Javiera Mena & Alex Torres
title: Co-located single display collaborative learning for early childhood education
summary_haiku: Small-group co-located single-display collaborative learning significantly improves oral language, logical-mathematical, and social skills in kindergarten children. Using a quasi-experimental design with 268 experimental and 172 control participants, researchers implemented computer-supported collaborative activities twice weekly for four months. Results showed the experimental group achieved substantially greater gains in logical-mathematical skills (21.78% vs. 6.09%) and social skills (10.09% vs. -8.19%), with teacher mediation proving essential for effective collaboration.

authors: Gahgene Gweon & Mahaveer Jain & John McDonough & Bhiksha Raj & Carolyn P. Rose
title: Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation
summary_haiku: Researchers developed an unsupervised Dynamic Bayesian Network model grounded in Speech Accommodation Theory to automatically detect other-oriented transactive contributions in dyadic speech discussions. Testing on debate recordings, they found significant positive correlation between automatic speech style accommodation measures and prevalence of other-oriented transacts (R=.36, p<.05), demonstrating that theoretically-informed computational models effectively assess collaborative learning processes.

authors: Gerry Stahl & Nancy Law & Friedrich Hesse
title: Collaborative Learning at CSCL 2013
summary_haiku: The CSCL 2013 conference brought together international researchers to advance collaborative learning research and practice. A presidential symposium analyzed regional developments in North America, Europe, Australia, and Asia, revealing diverse research approaches unified by a common goal: improving collaborative learning implementation in education. The field faces opportunities through initiatives like PISA's planned assessment of collaborative problem-solving skills.

authors: Raija Hamalainen & Bram De Wever
title: Vocational education approach: New TEL settings—new prospects for teachers’ instructional activities?
summary_haiku: This design-based research study examined vocational teachers' instructional activities in a 3D game environment using content analysis of 8,188 utterances from four teacher-student groups. Findings revealed teachers employed two distinct approaches: "knowledge-providing" and "joint problem-solving," with different student responses. Teachers asked more contextual questions and engaged in shared problem-solving than students, while students provided more knowledge. The study demonstrates teachers spontaneously develop innovative instructional strategies in technology-enhanced vocational learning settings, shifting from classroom management toward empowering collaborative knowledge construction.

authors: Annika Lantz-Andersson & Sylvi Vigmo & Rhonwen Bowen
title: Crossing boundaries in Facebook: Students’ framing of language learning activities as extended spaces
summary_haiku: This ethnographic case study examined how 60 students aged 13-16 from four countries framed English language learning activities in a Facebook group. Using frame analysis and sociocultural theory, researchers found that students initially adopted formal school-task framing but gradually negotiated boundary-crossing interactions creating extended learning spaces. However, maintaining these dynamic spaces proved difficult, requiring deliberate collaborative negotiation between educators and students to balance everyday social media practices with educational goals.

authors: Meng Yew Tee & Shuh Shing Lee
title: Advancing understanding using Nonaka’s model of knowledge creation and problem-based learning
summary_haiku: Integrating Nonaka's knowledge creation model with problem-based learning addresses Bereiter's critique that the model neglects understanding. This design-based research examined a 14-week course for in-service teachers developing technological pedagogical content knowledge. Findings demonstrate that combining socialization, externalization, combination, and internalization processes within problem-based learning phases cultivates advancing understanding of complex teaching-technology integration challenges.

authors: Armin Weinberger & Miika Marttunen & Leena Laurinen
title: Inducing socio-cognitive conflict in Finnish and German groups of online learners by CSCL script
summary_haiku: This cross-cultural study examined how a peer-critique collaboration script affects socio-cognitive conflict in online learning. Using a 2×2 design with 132 Finnish and German university students, researchers analyzed discussion patterns and knowledge acquisition. Results revealed German groups engaged in more conflict-oriented consensus building than Finnish groups, who preferred integration-oriented approaches. The script strengthened conflict-oriented discourse in German groups but proved incompatible with Finnish collaborative norms, suggesting CSCL environments require culturally sensitive design.

authors: M. Beatrice Ligorio & Fedela Feldia Loperfido & Nadia Sansone
title: Dialogical positions as a method of understanding identity trajectories in a collaborative blended university course
summary_haiku: # Summary This study proposes a three-step qualitative-quantitative method for tracking identity trajectories in collaborative learning using Bakhtinian concepts of polyphony and chronotopes as dialogical indicators. Applied to online notes from two university students in a blended course, the method reveals unique, context-sensitive identity development patterns, demonstrating how students' positioning shifts across course modules in response to activities and personal circumstances.

authors: Gerry Stahl & Nancy Law & Friedrich Hesse
title: Reigniting CSCL flash themes
summary_haiku: This editorial introduces four emerging research themes in computer-supported collaborative learning: eye-tracking for joint attention, argumentation in gaming contexts, scripting with awareness prompts for collaborative drawing, and learning analytics with tabletop interfaces. The authors critically examine these studies, emphasizing that CSCL research must remain fundamentally concerned with human meaning-making practices mediated through designed artifacts, regardless of methodological sophistication.

authors: Bertrand Schneider & Roy Pea
title: Real-time mutual gaze perception enhances collaborative learning and collaboration quality
summary_haiku: Real-time gaze visualization during remote collaborative learning on neuroscience contrasting cases enhanced learning gains and collaboration quality compared to control conditions. Eye-tracking enabled dyads to achieve higher joint attention, with followers benefiting most. Joint attention emerged as the primary mediator of improved learning outcomes.

authors: Esra Alagoz
title: Social argumentation in online synchronous communication
summary_haiku: This study examined argumentative practices among adolescents in World of Warcraft synchronous guild chat using ethnographic methods. Analysis of 27 argumentative exchanges revealed that 81% employed counter-critiques—stronger arguments directly refuting opponents' claims—rather than weaker counter-alternatives. Quality argumentation peaked during discussions about avatar customization (race/class, gear, talent builds), suggesting that interest-driven, authentic contexts where players exercise control over personalization trigger sophisticated argumentative discourse skills.

authors: Hannie Gijlers & Armin Weinberger & Alieke Mattia van Dijk & Lars Bollen & Wouter van Joolingen
title: Collaborative drawing on a shared digital canvas in elementary science education: The effects of script and task awareness support
summary_haiku: This study examined how scripting and task awareness support affect elementary students' collaborative drawing on photosynthesis. Ninety-four fifth-graders worked in dyads using a shared digital canvas under three conditions: control, awareness prompts, or structured script. Both support types increased transactive discourse and deeper conceptual understanding compared to controls. Scripted students acquired significantly more conceptual knowledge, while awareness and scripting both facilitated integrative consensus-building and process-related discussions.

authors: Roberto Martinez-Maldonado & Yannis Dimitriadis & Alejandra Martinez-Mones & Judy Kay & Kalina Yacef
title: Capturing and analyzing verbal and physical collaborative learning interactions at an enriched interactive tabletop
summary_haiku: This study developed an approach to automatically capture and analyze verbal and physical interactions at an enriched interactive tabletop to distinguish collaborative from less collaborative student groups. Using sequence pattern mining on data from 60 students in concept-mapping triads, the researchers identified interaction patterns—including speech timing, turn-taking, and peer engagement—that differentiated high from low collaboration groups, demonstrating the potential of multimodal data analysis for supporting collaborative learning awareness.

authors: Gerry Stahl & Ulrike Cress & Nancy Law & Sten Ludvigsen
title: Analyzing the multidimensional construction of knowledge in diverse contexts
summary_haiku: This editorial examines how knowledge is constructed across multiple levels—individual, small-group, and community—in diverse learning contexts. Through Activity Theory, knowledge-building games, Knowledge Forum analysis, and Wikipedia research, the authors demonstrate that collaborative knowledge construction relies on interactional resources and artifacts that bridge different analytical scales, from classroom discourse to global online communities.

authors: Sue Timmis
title: The dialectical potential of Cultural Historical Activity Theory for researching sustainable CSCL practices
summary_haiku: Cultural Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) offers a relational, dialectical framework for understanding sustainable computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) in authentic educational settings. This study proposes an integrated CHAT methodology that moves beyond descriptive triangle models to analyze contradictions and tensions across multiple activity levels. Through a five-stage analytical process applied to undergraduate online collaboration, the research demonstrates how CHAT's dialectical method reveals complex interrelations between discourse, actions, and community, explaining why collaborative practices succeed or fail to become institutionalized.

authors: Katerine Bielaczyc & John Ow
title: Multi-player epistemic games: Guiding the enactment of classroom knowledge-building communities
summary_haiku: Researchers extended epistemic games—strategic knowledge-building practices—to "multi-player" versions where students collectively advance ideas through distributed contributions in Knowledge Forum. Using design-based research in Singapore primary science classrooms, they developed scaffolding tools (Think Cards and hypothetical game-configurations) to help students learn the Progressive-Improvement Game. Analyses showed students improved significantly in generating valid knowledge-building moves, supporting classroom enactment of knowledge-building communities.

authors: Iassen Halatchliyski & Johannes Moskaliuk & Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress
title: Explaining authors’ contribution to pivotal artifacts during mass collaboration in the Wikipedia’s knowledge base
summary_haiku: This empirical study examined how authors' contribution experience relates to their involvement in pivotal Wikipedia articles across two knowledge domains. Using network analysis on German Wikipedia data, researchers identified two types of pivotal articles: those central within single domains and those bridging domains. Results showed domain specialists predominantly contributed to domain-central articles, while generalists contributed to boundary-crossing articles. Article experience positively predicted contributions to both article types regardless of specialization.

authors: Gerry Stahl & Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen & Nancy Law
title: Dialogic foundations of CSCL
summary_haiku: Dialogical theory, rooted in Vygotsky and Bakhtin's work, provides essential foundations for CSCL by emphasizing that cognition and meaning-making emerge through social interaction rather than individual minds. This editorial examines four empirical studies employing different methodologies—from dialogical discourse analysis to controlled experiments—demonstrating that CSCL research thrives through complementary theoretical and methodological approaches to understanding collaborative learning processes.

authors: Stefan Trausan-Matu & Mihai Dascalu
title: PolyCAFe—automatic support for the polyphonic analysis of CSCL chats
summary_haiku: PolyCAFe applies the polyphonic framework—grounded in Bakhtin's dialogism and musical metaphor—to automatically analyze collaborative learning chats. Using Natural Language Processing and Social Network Analysis, the system identifies implicit links between utterances, detects voices and their inter-animations, and generates quantitative metrics for collaboration assessment. Evaluation experiments demonstrate that PolyCAFe significantly reduces tutor feedback preparation time while providing useful insights to learners about their participation.

authors: Benzi Slakmon & Baruch B. Schwarz
title: Disengaged students and dialogic learning: the role of CSCL affordances
summary_haiku: This study examines how three disengaged eighth-grade students gradually adopted dialogic norms through participation in computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) discussions using the Argunaut tool. Through temporal analysis of philosophical discussions, the research demonstrates that peer-mediated exposure to dialogic practices—rather than direct teacher intervention—enabled students to develop multivoicedness and expand their discursive repertoires. CSCL affordances, including delayed responses and reduced prosodic cues, facilitated this transformation.

authors: Alyssa Friend Wise & Simone Nicole Hausknecht & Yuting Zhao
title: Attending to others’ posts in asynchronous discussions: Learners’ online “listening” and its relationship to speaking
summary_haiku: Students' depth of listening—specifically rereading peers' posts—positively predicts responsiveness and argumentation quality in online discussions, while breadth alone does not. Using clickstream data from 31 undergraduates across six asynchronous discussions, multi-level regressions revealed that revisiting others' posts predicted more responsive comments, and reading (versus scanning) posts predicted richer argumentation. These listening-speaking relationships manifested differently across learner types over time.

authors: Tanja Engelmann & Richard Kolodziej & Friedrich W. Hesse
title: Preventing undesirable effects of mutual trust and the development of skepticism in virtual groups by applying the knowledge and information awareness approach
summary_haiku: This experimental study examined whether a knowledge and information awareness (KIA) approach—providing digital concept maps of collaborators' knowledge—mitigates negative effects of mutual trust in virtual groups. Comparing 40 triads (20 with KIA, 20 without), researchers found that high initial trust reduced effectiveness in control groups but not experimental groups, while both conditions showed equal efficiency gains. Additionally, poor collaboration quality increased skepticism in control groups but not experimental groups, suggesting KIA facilitates mutual control independent of trust levels.

authors: G. Stahl & S. Ludvigsen & N. Law & U. Cress
title: CSCL artifacts
summary_haiku: Artifacts are central to computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL), serving multiple roles including communication media, knowledge representation structures, and collaborative products. This editorial examines how artifacts mediate group meaning-making processes and presents four papers analyzing artifact roles in CSCL settings and trends in CSCL research publications, advancing understanding of the post-cognitive CSCL paradigm emphasizing group-level processes over individual learning outcomes.

authors: Crina Damsa
title: The multi-layered nature of small-group learning: Productive interactions in object-oriented collaboration
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examines productive interactions in small-group collaborative learning through a 20-week undergraduate research project. Using qualitative analysis and descriptive statistics, the researcher analyzed five student groups' interactions and emerging knowledge objects (research reports). Findings reveal that productive interactions manifest in two primary patterns: discourse-based interactions fostering shared understanding, and object-oriented interactions involving iterative co-construction. Groups demonstrating shared epistemic agency—deliberate, joint engagement with knowledge materialization—produced higher-quality knowledge objects, suggesting that productive collaboration integrates discursive interaction with tangible object development over time.

authors: Maarten Overdijk & Wouter van Diggelen & Jerry Andriessen & Paul A. Kirschner
title: How to bring a technical artifact into use: A micro-developmental perspective
summary_haiku: # Summary This micro-developmental case study examines how a student pair appropriated a digital shared workspace for project planning. Using qualitative analysis of classroom observations, interviews, and interaction protocols, the research reveals that artifact appropriation involves tension between existing classroom practices and new tool affordances. Resistance from the artifact—when it contradicted established planning conventions—triggered reflection and procedural adaptation, while absence of resistance enabled unreflective departures from regular practice. The findings demonstrate that technology use emerges through complex negotiations between learner intentions and designer intentions embedded in artifacts.

authors: Heisawn Jeong & Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver & Yawen Yu
title: An examination of CSCL methodological practices and the influence of theoretical frameworks 2005–2009
summary_haiku: This content analysis examined methodological practices in 400 empirical CSCL studies published 2005–2009 across seven leading journals. Researchers coded studies across research designs, settings, data sources, and analysis methods, then examined relationships with theoretical frameworks. Findings revealed descriptive designs dominated (54%), classroom settings predominated (74%), and quantitative analysis was most common (86%), though qualitative and mixed methods were frequent. Cluster analysis identified four distinctive method-theory combinations, demonstrating that theoretical frameworks significantly influenced methodological choices across all dimensions.

authors: Kai-Yu Tang & Chin-Chung Tsai & Tzu-Chiang Lin
title: Contemporary intellectual structure of CSCL research (2006–2013): a co-citation network analysis with an education focus
summary_haiku: This study employed document co-citation analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and social network analysis to map the intellectual structure of CSCL research (2006–2013). Analyzing 403 source papers and 5,351 citing articles, researchers identified six research subfields: representation and discourse patterns, factors influencing CSCL, intervention and comparison, critical reasoning, social construction processes, and design and modeling. Results revealed seminal works and core publications, with representation and discourse emerging as the dominant research stream, demonstrating the field's maturity and interconnectedness.

authors: Gerry Stahl & Nancy Law & Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen
title: Analyzing roles of individuals in small-group collaboration processes
summary_haiku: This editorial examines how computer-supported collaborative learning research analyzes individual roles within small groups. Four empirical studies employ diverse methodologies—eye-tracking analysis, interaction coding, social network analysis, and discourse analysis—to investigate joint attention, leadership, social roles, and uncertainty expressions. The papers collectively demonstrate that collaborative learning processes operate at multiple analytical levels, with group-level phenomena like shared intentionality and collective agency irreducible to individual cognition alone.

authors: Bertrand Schneider & Roy Pea
title: Toward collaboration sensing
summary_haiku: Researchers applied network analysis to dual eye-tracking data from collaborative learning dyads, representing fixations as nodes and saccades as edges. Network metrics correlated with collaboration quality dimensions, and machine learning algorithms predicted collaboration quality with 85-100% accuracy, suggesting eye-tracking networks can serve as "collaboration-sensing" tools for assessing and potentially improving student teamwork.

authors: Emma M. Mercier & Steven E. Higgins & Laura da Costa
title: Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children’s collaborative learning groups
summary_haiku: This study examines emergent leadership in children's collaborative learning groups through two investigations. Using a coding scheme adapted from prior research, the authors analyzed 32 students in Study One and 96 students in Study Two, identifying leadership moves as either intellectual (idea development, topic control) or organizational (turn management, planning). Results reveal leadership is distributed among group members, with approximately half of groups showing distinct intellectual and organizational leaders held by different students. Leadership patterns vary significantly across content areas and task types, suggesting leadership is context-dependent rather than stable.

authors: H. Smith Risser & SueAnn Bottoms
title: “Newbies” and “Celebrities”: Detecting social roles in an online network of teachers via participation patterns
summary_haiku: This study used cluster analysis combining structural and behavioral data to identify social roles in an unstructured online teacher blog network. Analyzing 99 teachers' participation patterns across six months, researchers detected five distinct roles: "Newbies," "Inbound Participants," "Full Participants," "Celebrities," and "Peripheral Members." Results revealed that participation patterns and network position significantly influence both current role and trajectory of role change, with expertise and engagement type affecting status transitions independent of tenure.

authors: Michelle E. Jordan & An-Chih Janne Cheng & Diane Schallert & Kwangok Song & SoonAh Lee & Yangjoo Park
title: “I guess my question is”: What is the co-occurrence of uncertainty and learning in computer-mediated discourse?
summary_haiku: This study examined how uncertainty expressions and learning co-occur in graduate students' computer-mediated discussions. Using inductive coding of 1,048 comments across synchronous and asynchronous online discussions, researchers found that 72% of paragraphs containing uncertainty also exhibited learning markers. Direct uncertainty expressions correlated with presenting new ideas and applications, while indirect expressions associated more with elaboration. Results suggest uncertainty expression facilitates productive learning through collaborative meaning-making in online environments.

authors: Sten Ludvigsen & Gerry Stahl & Nancy Law & Ulrike Cress
title: From the editors: Collaboration and the formation of new knowledge artifacts
summary_haiku: Computer-supported collaborative learning fundamentally involves creating and refining knowledge artifacts—physical or virtual objects embodying shared meanings. This editorial examines how collaborative technologies enable students to construct intersubjective understanding through artifacts like augmented-reality environments, texts, visualizations, and networked tools, emphasizing that productive learning emerges from alignment between conceptual resources and material structures during collaborative interaction.

authors: Noel Enyedy & Joshua A. Danish & David DeLiema
title: Constructing liminal blends in a collaborative augmented-reality learning environment
summary_haiku: This study examines how augmented-reality environments support physics learning through "liminal blends"—conceptual integrations of students' embodied experiences, physical materials, peer contributions, and symbolic representations. Using interaction analysis of second-graders learning about friction, the researchers demonstrate how students blend their bodies, game narratives, material surfaces, and AR symbols to reason about force and motion, revealing cognition as distributed across individuals, materials, and social interaction.

authors: Andrea Forte
title: The new information literate: Open collaboration and information production in schools
summary_haiku: This qualitative study examined high school students' information assessment practices while contributing to a collaborative online wiki. Through 57 interviews and classroom observations, the researcher identified two information literacy strategies: first-order strategies involving established heuristics for evaluating sources, and second-order strategies involving reflective analysis of how information is produced. Findings reveal that participating in information production enhanced students' understanding of source credibility and fostered individual responsibility for contributing accurate information to public resources.

authors: Pryce Davis & Michael Horn & Florian Block & Brenda Phillips & E. Margaret Evans & Judy Diamond & Chia Shen
title: Whoa! We’re going deep in the trees!: Patterns of collaboration around an interactive information visualization exhibit
summary_haiku: This study analyzed how child dyads collaboratively explored DeepTree, an interactive multi-touch tabletop exhibit visualizing 70,000+ species in a phylogenetic tree. Using qualitative interaction analysis of museum visitors, researchers identified four distinct collaboration patterns organized by coordination level and action target: reactive, autonomous, planning, and contemplative. Results showed that DeepTree supported learning of macroevolutionary concepts like common descent, with design features like the "fly-through" mechanic facilitating meaning-making across different interaction patterns.

authors: Yun Wen & Chee-Kit Looi & Wenli Chen
title: Appropriation of a representational tool in a second-language classroom
summary_haiku: This case study examined how secondary school students appropriated Group Scribbles, a representational tool, during collaborative Chinese-language writing in a networked classroom. Through microanalysis of cross-media interactions between face-to-face and online spaces, researchers identified five functions inscriptional devices served in group-understanding development: referencing, pinpointing, prompting notice, realizing parallels, and promoting synergy. Findings revealed that representational tools supplement face-to-face communication by enabling balanced participation, helping learners notice linguistic problems, and serving as resources for elaborating ideas.

authors: Ulrike Cress & Gerry Stahl & Sten Ludvigsen & classroom orchestration. The
title: The core features of CSCL: Social situation, collaborative knowledge processes and their design
summary_haiku: This editorial examines three core CSCL features: how social situations influence collaboration, the nature of collaborative knowledge processes, and effective design of learning environments.
