authors: Anders I. Mørch & Renate Andersen & Siv Eie & Louise Mifsud
title: Emergent group understanding: Investigating intersubjectivity in sociotechnical interdependencies
summary_haiku: This study investigates how shared understanding emerges in computer-mediated learning using Minecraft for social studies. Through design-based research with student teachers reconstructing historical industrial sites, researchers identified "emergent group understanding"—a phenomenon where spontaneous individual knowledge contributions trigger focused group action toward shared learning goals. The framework integrates sociotechnical congruence, intersubjectivity, and emergence theories, revealing how social and technological objects co-evolve through six states of intersubjectivity toward knowledge objects.

authors: Mariel Miller & Allyson F. Hadwin
title: Comparing the effectiveness of CSCL scripts for shared task perceptions in socially shared regulation of collaborative learning
summary_haiku: High-support group planning scripts significantly improved undergraduate students' accuracy of shared task perceptions and transactive planning discussions compared to low-support scripts, though individual-level support showed no detectable effect. However, enhanced task perceptions did not translate to improved group performance, suggesting groups may struggle to implement shared understanding during task execution.

authors: Tenchita Alzaga Elizondo & David Brown
title: Students’ use of technological tools to engage in collective mathematical proof activity
summary_haiku: Using instrumental genesis theory, this study examined how students in a remote introduction to proofs course operationalized Google Docs and Zoom to engage in collaborative proof activity. Analysis of six episodes revealed students developed collective utilization schemes coordinating visual mediators with verbal communication to enable collective argumentation and co-construct solutions through iterative text refinement. Google Docs' simultaneous editing and referencing features particularly supported active, process-oriented proof writing.

authors: M. Borge & B. K. Smith & T. Aldemir
title: Using generative ai as a simulation to support higher‑order thinking
summary_haiku: # Summary This case study examines whether generative AI can support higher-order thinking through human-computer collaboration. An expert in collaborative learning engaged in extended dialogue with ChatGPT, practicing metacognitive and sociometacognitive skills while reflecting on interaction quality using a framework of six communication patterns. Findings indicate ChatGPT feasibly supports both individual metacognition and collective sensemaking when users actively regulate conversations and employ structured reflection prompts, though limitations like tendency toward definitive unsupported claims require human oversight for effective learning.

authors: Michael Baker & Peter Reimann
title: Editorial notes: Unity in diversity at the CSCL crossroads
summary_haiku: # Summary This editorial examines whether CSCL constitutes a unified scientific field or an interdisciplinary crossroads. Rather than seeking a single unifying framework, the authors argue CSCL exhibits "family resemblances"—partial commonalities across diverse theoretical and methodological approaches. Four featured articles demonstrate this diversity through temporal analysis of collaborative problem-solving, role dynamics, stance-taking in programming, and scripting/reflection scaffolding, collectively illustrating how CSCL research maintains creative vitality through methodological pluralism.

authors: Ramy Elmoazen & Mohammed Saqr & Laura Hirsto & Matti Tedre
title: Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry
summary_haiku: This longitudinal study analyzed 135 dental students' online problem-based learning discussions across four courses using Community of Inquiry framework coding combined with latent class analysis, epistemic network analysis, and process mining. Three distinct roles emerged: leaders, social mediators, and peripheral explorers. Students exhibited stable role trajectories across time, with active trajectories achieving higher grades than free riders, suggesting roles function as stable dispositions requiring intentional teacher intervention for change.

authors: Sebastian Strauss & Isis Tunnigkeit & Julia Eberle & Arlind Avdullahu & Nikol Rummel
title: Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction
summary_haiku: This experimental study compared external collaboration scripts and reflection scaffolds for fostering collaboration skills in 150 university students working in groups. Using multilevel modeling, researchers found that learners receiving collaborative reflection gained significantly more knowledge about effective collaboration than those using scripts or no support. However, neither intervention improved subsequent interaction quality. Results suggest reflection-based approaches may offer autonomy-supportive alternatives to directive scripting for knowledge acquisition.

authors: Morgan M. Fong & David DeLiema & Virginia J. Flood & Oia Walker-van Aalst
title: Correction: Contesting sociocomputational norms: computer programming instructors and students’ stancetaking around refactoring
summary_haiku: This correction clarifies a discrepancy in the theoretical framework section of an interaction analysis study examining how computer programming instructors and students contest sociocomputational norms through classroom discourse. The researchers use stancetaking analysis to investigate participatory and relational inequities without assuming participants' inner experiences, focusing on how meanings are publicly negotiated.

authors: Laura Brandl & Matthias Stadler & Constanze Richters & Anika Radkowitsch & Martin R. Fischer & Ralf Schmidmaier & Frank Fischer
title: Correction: Collaborative Problem‑Solving in Knowledge‑Rich Domains: A Multi‑Study Structural Equation Model
summary_haiku: This is a correction notice for a structural equation modeling study examining collaborative problem-solving in knowledge-rich domains. The original article contained a sign error in Table 5, where most coefficients were incorrectly prefixed with negative signs. The corrected version has been published online.

authors: Morgan M. Fong & David DeLiema & Virginia J. Flood & Oia Walker-van Aalst
title: Contesting sociocomputational norms: Computer programming instructors and students’ stancetaking around refactoring
summary_haiku: This interaction analysis study examines how elementary and middle school students and instructors negotiate refactoring—revising working code—in a programming workshop. Using stancetaking, sociocomputational norms, and inequity frameworks, researchers analyzed 20 minutes of classroom discourse. Findings reveal that while students initially debated coding approaches, instructors progressively endorsed loops as superior, amplifying relational inequity by devaluing alternative strategies and limiting discussion of efficiency's multiple interpretations.

authors: Shuowen An & Si Zhang & Zhihui Cai & Wei Pan & Mingwei Li & Mingwen Tong
title: Revealing the interplay of cognitive, meta‑cognitive, and social processes in university students’ collaborative problem solving: a three‑stage analytical framework
summary_haiku: This study proposes a three-stage analytical framework to examine collaborative problem-solving (CPS) patterns among 24 university students completing instructional design and multimedia development tasks. Using dynamic time warping for clustering and process mining analysis, the researchers identified two distinct CPS subgroups: solution-driven groups that effectively transitioned from divergent to convergent thinking through meta-cognitive monitoring, and problem-driven groups that focused on task requirements but lacked comprehensive evaluation processes, resulting in lower performance outcomes.

authors: Michael Baker & Peter Reimann
title: Editorial notes: Core issues in CSCL research
summary_haiku: This editorial examines four core CSCL research issues: task design effects on collaboration and learning, dialogue and disagreement in knowledge co-elaboration, and technology mediation. Studies compared conceptual versus hands-on physics tasks, analyzed maritime simulator training, tracked belief change across multiple debates, and investigated how direct versus soft disagreement affects peer critique. Findings emphasize that task authenticity, dialogue quality, and disagreement management significantly influence collaborative learning outcomes.

authors: Kateryna Zabolotna & Liv Nøhr & Megumi Iwata & Daniel Spikol & Jonna Malmberg & Hanna Jarvenoja
title: How does collaborative task design shape collaborative knowledge construction and group‑level regulation of learning? A study of secondary school students’ interactions in two varied tasks
summary_haiku: Task design significantly shapes collaborative learning processes. This study compared a conceptual physics drawing task and a hands-on robotics task involving secondary students, analyzing collaborative knowledge construction and group-level regulation using video coding and network analysis. Conceptually oriented tasks promoted prolonged cognitive engagement and stronger connections between cognitive regulation and negotiation, while hands-on tasks featured frequent but brief knowledge construction episodes emphasizing socioemotional interactions for maintaining collaboration.

authors: Charlott Sellberg & Amit Sharma
title: Toward multimodal learning analytics in simulation‑based collaborative learning: A design ethnography of maritime training
summary_haiku: # Summary This design ethnography examines maritime simulator-based training to inform multimodal learning analytics (MMLA) development. Through detailed video analysis of master mariner students' collaborative bridge activities, the researchers identified how instructors deliver embedded assessments and feedback using multiple social and material resources. The study proposes specific technologies—system logs, eye-tracking, and speech recognition—necessary for capturing professional performance, communication, and collaboration in simulation-based learning environments.

authors: Jinzhi Zhou & Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver & Zach Ryan & Christina Stiso & Danielle Murphy & Joshua Danish & Clark A. Chinn & Ravit Golan Duncan
title: Disagreeing softly: Supporting students in managing disagreement in peer critique
summary_haiku: Fifth-grade students engaged in peer critique within a computer-supported collaborative learning environment predominantly used soft disagreements (64%) rather than direct forms when critiquing groupmates' scientific models. Using conversation analysis, researchers found that students effectively resolved disagreements consensually in 88.6% of episodes, advancing collective knowledge through both direct and soft disagreement forms, while maintaining positive group dynamics.

authors: Jauwairia Nasir & Aditi Kothiyal & Barbara Bruno & Pierre Dillenbourg
title: Correction to: Many are the ways to learn: Identifying multi‑modal behavioral profiles of collaborative learning in constructivist activities
summary_haiku: This correction document addresses formatting and citation errors in the original 2021 article examining multi-modal behavioral profiles in collaborative constructivist learning. The researchers identified and corrected a missing colon in the title and multiple misattributed or incorrectly formatted citations throughout the paper, ensuring accurate reference to their prior work on collaborative learning analytics.

authors: Fan Ouyang & Weiqi Xu & Mutlu Cukurova
title: Correction: An artificial intelligence‑driven learning analytics method to examine the collaborative problem‑solving process from the complex adaptive systems perspective
summary_haiku: This is a correction notice for an article on artificial intelligence-driven learning analytics examining collaborative problem-solving through complex adaptive systems theory. The correction addresses an erroneous figure that appeared in the original publication, replacing it with the correct framework diagram of complex adaptive systems theory adapted from Holland's work.

authors: Deanna Kuhn & Teresa Fraguada & Mariel Halpern
title: How do new ideas come to be adopted during discourse?
summary_haiku: This study examines how adolescents adopt and revise ideas during electronic peer argumentation. Two case studies traced participants' evolving positions across eight successive dialogs on juvenile justice. Results revealed contrasting patterns: one participant readily adopted partners' ideas but struggled defending positions, while the other maintained firm beliefs with strong counterargument skills but limited openness to new ideas. Findings highlight how argumentation skills, epistemological understanding, and metacognitive reflection jointly influence belief change in collaborative discourse.

authors: Michael Baker & Peter Reimann
title: Editorial notes: Extending perennial topics in CSCL
summary_haiku: This editorial examines how CSCL research extends perennial topics through technological innovation and theoretical advancement. Papers address reflective dialogue using visualization and immersive virtual reality, collaboration quality assessment via self-evaluation scales, and dialogue analysis through positioning theory. The editors argue that balancing theoretical expansion with knowledge accumulation across established themes strengthens the field's scientific foundations.

authors: Pengjin Wang & Fan Chen & Deliang Wang & Gaowei Chen
title: Enhancing students’ dialogic reflection through classroom discourse visualisation
summary_haiku: Visualisation-supported dialogic reflection (VSDR) using classroom discourse analysis enhanced primary students' collaborative learning. A 3-month intervention with 53 students showed significant knowledge gains in the high-dose group and increased student participation across both groups. Qualitative analysis revealed students engaged in deeper reflection on problem-solving strategies, group collaboration, and whole-class participation when reviewing visualised classroom discourse through discussion forums.

authors: Lucas Paulsen & Jacob Davidsen
title: Activity‑based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning
summary_haiku: Paulsen and Davidsen propose Activity-Based Collaborative Virtual Reality (ABC-VR), a conceptual framework grounded in activity theory for designing and researching collaborative learning in immersive 360-degree video environments. Unlike existing individual-focused concepts, ABC-VR emphasizes social knowledge construction through analyzing recorded real-world activities at multiple levels—examining what actions occur, how they're performed, and why. The framework positions learners collaboratively engaging with situated practices from educational, social, and work contexts.

authors: Loris T. Jeitziner & Lisa Paneth & Oliver Rack & Susanne Bleisch & Carmen Zahn
title: Measuring the quality of collaborative group engagement: Development and validation of the QCGE self‑assessment scale (QCGE‑SAS)
summary_haiku: This study developed and validated the QCGE-SAS, a 13-item self-assessment scale measuring quality of collaborative group engagement across four dimensions: behavioral, social, cognitive, and conceptual-to-consequential engagement. Using confirmatory factor analysis with 246 higher education students, the scale demonstrated good model fit and construct validity through correlations with related measures. Three subscales showed acceptable reliability; however, the social engagement subscale exhibited suboptimal internal consistency, warranting future refinement.

authors: Aaron J. Peltoniemi & Joni Lamsa & Sami Lehesvuori
title: Understanding the role of I‑positions facilitating knowledge construction in a computer‑supported collaborative learning environment
summary_haiku: This qualitative study applies discourse analysis and dialogical self theory to investigate how interpersonal and intrapersonal voices facilitate knowledge construction in computer-supported collaborative learning. Analyzing ten physics students in two groups, researchers identified discourse functions and I-positions (I–it, I–me, I–you, I–we) within dialogues. The successful group employed both interpersonal and intrapersonal voices, with intrapersonal voices peaking during empirical evaluation, while the unsuccessful group relied predominantly on interpersonal voices focused on individual-level concerns rather than collective elaboration.

authors: Sten Ludvigsen & Hans C. Arnseth & Kenneth Silseth & Rolf Steier
title: Collaborative science? Formalism and a unified language: Future directions for computer‑supported collaborative learning
summary_haiku: # Summary This article responds to calls for unified language and formalism in computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL). Rather than endorsing computational modeling approaches, the authors propose a meta-stance centered on learning mechanisms that integrate cognitive, socio-cognitive, and sociocultural perspectives. They advocate for analyzing moment-by-moment meaning-making through dialogue, mediational tools, and meaning potentials, arguing this approach better captures collaborative learning processes than probabilistic models alone. The authors present an exchange structure formalism and emphasize mechanistic causality in qualitative research to build cumulative CSCL knowledge.

authors: Peter Reimann & Michael J. Baker
title: Editorial notes: Mechanisms as a unifying construct for CSCL research
summary_haiku: This editorial proposes mechanistic explanation as a unifying framework for CSCL research. Drawing on realist philosophy of science, the authors argue that identifying generative mechanisms—organized configurations producing outcomes through spatiotemporal continuity—provides deeper explanations than variable-based approaches. They illustrate this through stratification in collaborative learning, demonstrating how Directed Acyclic Graphs and Bayesian Networks model causal relationships, while agent-based modeling captures micro-to-macro mechanisms linking individual actions to group outcomes.

authors: Shihui Feng & Ziyi Wei
title: The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review
summary_haiku: This systematic review of 66 studies (2005-2024) proposes the CoMPAS framework for modeling individual participation in collaborative learning using process data. The framework identifies six forms of participation—cognitive interactions, coordinative interactions, metacognitive interactions, passive participation, solo active participation, and socio-emotional interactions—analyzed through oral conversational, textual, log, and nonverbal physical data using descriptive, content, network, and clustering methods. Findings reveal bidirectional relationships between individual participation and group performance.

authors: Alena Seredko
title: Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow
summary_haiku: # Summary This study investigates how software developers collaboratively frame programming problems on Stack Overflow through asynchronous, fluid participation. Using trace ethnography and sequential analysis of selected threads, the research reveals that minimal reproducible examples (MREs) structured within the platform's dual-space design enable collaboration at scale. Standardized norm-enforcing requests and explicit referencing practices ensure mutual intelligibility among unknown contributors, facilitating effective problem-solving in large-scale online environments.

authors: Shigen Shimojo & Yugo Hayashi
title: Age‑related differences in explanatory activities during collaborative learning with concept maps: experimental investigation using epistemic network analysis
summary_haiku: Younger adults demonstrated significantly higher learning performance and concept map quality than older adults during collaborative learning with concept maps using attribution theory. While younger adults engaged more frequently in active utterances and showed stronger connections between constructive and interactive behaviors, older adults exhibited higher constructive and interactive utterance frequencies but stronger active-interactive connections. Epistemic network analysis revealed that older adults required knowledge reactivation during elaboration, suggesting age-related cognitive decline hinders knowledge integration in computer-supported collaborative learning environments.

authors: Changhao Liang & Yuko Toyokawa & Hiroaki Ogata
title: Optimizing group formation with a mixed genetic algorithm: an empirical study in active reading using marker data
summary_haiku: A mixed genetic algorithm embedded in a learning platform optimizes group formation for EFL active reading by balancing homogeneous and heterogeneous student characteristics using marker data. Implemented in a Japanese high school classroom with 39 students, the system significantly improved vocabulary learning gains and demonstrated positive group dynamics through Wordcloud visualization, with 85% of students reporting the tool's helpfulness for collaborative tasks.

authors: Azzeddine Benabbou & Catherine Pons
title: Collaboration in virtual and remote laboratories for education: A systematic literature review
summary_haiku: This systematic literature review examined 62 educational virtual and remote laboratories published 2011-2025 to assess collaboration support. While communication and group awareness tools are well-integrated, guidance and regulation tools remain underrepresented. Most laboratories support synchronous, non-co-located collaboration in STEM disciplines. Evaluation studies show predominantly positive learning outcomes, yet only one-third assess collaboration quality, indicating a significant research gap requiring future investigation.

authors: Michael J. Baker & Peter Reimann
title: Editorial notes: Collaboration, feedback and dynamics
summary_haiku: This editorial examines foundational CSCL concepts through five empirical papers. It explores whether collaboration extends to human-AI interactions and large-group collective intelligence, reconceptualizes feedback as multimodal and embodied rather than unidirectional, and argues that describing collaborative dynamics requires deeper ontological models beyond flat variable relationships—integrating layered processes, functional analysis, and mechanist explanations to understand how learning actually emerges.

authors: Tatiana Iniguez-Berrozpe & Carmen Elboj-Saso & Francesco Marcaletti
title: Learning to deal with hate speech: An online collective intelligence experiment on the Collective Learning platform
summary_haiku: This study examined whether collective intelligence can help adolescents manage online hate speech using the Collective Learning platform. Spanish teenagers (ages 15–16) were divided into one large group (n=123) and two smaller groups (n=18, n=23). Results showed that collective intelligence conditions emerged only in the large group, which demonstrated significant improvements in responses across four questions assessing moral reasoning and prosocial action regarding hate speech. Small groups showed minimal improvement, suggesting group size and heterogeneity are critical for collective intelligence to facilitate learning about hate speech prevention.

authors: Yifat Ben-David Kolikant & Omri Hadar & Asaf Salman
title: Talk to the machine: Unleashing the potential of AI to scale dialogic education and reduce polarization
summary_haiku: # Summary Researchers fine-tuned an LLM-based chatbot called LlamaLo on productive Reddit discussions to explore its potential for scaling dialogic education and reducing polarization. Through qualitative analysis of ten conversations on contentious topics, they found LlamaLo effectively opened dialogic spaces by questioning assumptions and presenting alternatives. However, challenges including negative tone, bias, and occasional incoherence could undermine dialogue and require computational and pedagogical solutions.

authors: Sarah Jaewon Lee & Xintian Tu & Simeon Adebola & D. Teo Keifert & Noel Enyedy & Joshua Danish
title: How children blend feedback in a mixed‑reality environment for collective embodied learning
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined how young children coordinate multiple feedback sources—self, peers, teachers, and technology—in a mixed-reality learning environment called STEP to understand states of matter. Using interaction analysis of three episodes (making solid, liquid, and gas bonds), researchers found that children progressively blended diverse feedback modalities to collectively construct scientific understanding while exercising agency over their inquiry process. The findings demonstrate that embodied, technology-enhanced environments supporting collective feedback structures enable young children to engage in sophisticated systems thinking earlier than traditionally expected.

authors: Jihong Ding & Zhihao Fan & Huazhong Liu & James Slotta & Feng Ji & Kefeng Hu
title: Understanding collaborative programming dynamics: The role of prior knowledge, engagement and ICAP learning modes
summary_haiku: This study examined collaborative programming through multimodal learning analytics, integrating four-dimensional engagement (behavioral, cognitive, social, emotional) with the ICAP framework. Analyzing 18 student triads, findings reveal prior knowledge supports individual task execution but requires strong leadership for collaborative engagement. Social and cognitive engagement strongly correlate, while emotional engagement remains largely independent. Interactive discourse modes foster significantly richer engagement and higher achievement than active modes, with social engagement and emotional regulation emerging as primary predictors of learning outcomes.

authors: Bertrand Schneider & Xiao Fang & Shinyi Kang & Pankaj Chejara & Jiajun Bu
title: A quarter century of advances in collaboration sensing: a comprehensive review of high‑frequency metrics and their connection to collaborative constructs from 2000 to 2025
summary_haiku: This systematic review of 163 studies (2000-2025) examines how multimodal sensing technologies capture collaboration through high-frequency metrics. Using the PRISMA framework and a construct-to-data mapping approach, researchers analyzed connections between sensor-derived metrics (verbal, gaze, body, physiological, head, log data) and collaborative indicators (coordination, performance, learning, engagement, affects). Key findings reveal most studies employed laboratory settings with small samples, relied on simple synchronization metrics, and lacked standardized measurement tools. Critically, less than 9% leveraged sensor data for real-time interventions, identifying major gaps in designing guidance systems beyond mirroring feedback.

authors: Michael J. Baker & Peter Reimann
title: Editorial Notes: the CSCL universe is still expanding
summary_haiku: This editorial examines four CSCL research papers addressing technology-mediated collaborative learning. Studies investigate anger's productive role in educational games, knowledge synthesis through technological artifacts, temporal network analysis revealing group regulatory patterns, and intergenerational learning in smart home environments. Findings demonstrate that emotional dynamics, meaning reification, temporal group dynamics, and expanded social contexts significantly influence collaborative learning outcomes, while the field continues expanding its analytical scope.

authors: Taehyun Kim & Mike Tissenbaum
title: Understanding when anger becomes productive or destructive in collaborative educational games
summary_haiku: Anger in collaborative game-based learning can facilitate productive discourse when students engage in reasoned debate about strategy and game mechanics. However, when anger escalates into "tilting"—characterized by emotional dysregulation, withdrawal, and abandonment of collaborative goals—it severely disrupts group performance. The study analyzed middle school students' interactions in City Settlers, finding that appropriately expressed anger drove deeper engagement with complex systems, while unresolved anger conflicts led to group breakdown.

authors: Xinran Zhu & Bodong Chen & David DeLiema
title: Advancing collaborative discourse through knowledge synthesis
summary_haiku: # Summary This study investigates a knowledge synthesis intervention designed to support collaborative discourse in a graduate course. Using qualitative methods including content and interaction analysis, researchers examined how students' individual synthesis artifacts—created from social annotations—facilitated group collaboration. Findings reveal that synthesis artifacts guided discourse progression, enabled key knowledge practices, and supported group artifact development, though effectiveness depended on both artifact quality and collaborative engagement patterns.

authors: Mohammed Saqr & Sonsoles Lopez-Pernas & Tiina Tormanen
title: A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration
summary_haiku: This study employs temporal network analysis combined with clustering, sequence analysis, and growth models to examine how online problem-based learning groups regulate collaboration over time. Analyzing 118 discussion groups, researchers identified four distinct weekly regulation patterns and found that groups using interactive socioemotional or regulated constructive patterns demonstrated higher cognitive productivity. Critically, explicit group regulation emerged infrequently and primarily in response to challenges, while most groups maintained stable patterns with minimal improvement over time, suggesting early instructional support is essential for fostering productive regulation.

authors: Mohammed Saqr & Sonsoles Lopez-Pernas
title: Correction: A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration
summary_haiku: This is a correction notice for a research article on temporal network analysis in computer-supported collaborative learning. The original study examined longitudinal dynamics of group regulation and productive collaboration using temporal network methods. The correction addresses a production error where Figure 2 inadvertently duplicated Figure 1, now providing the correct visualization to accurately represent the research findings.

authors: Ge Wang & Roy Pea
title: Co‑constructing critical data literacy in families: A technology‑mediated learning perspective
summary_haiku: # Summary This study investigates how families collaboratively develop critical data literacy about smart home technologies through FamiData Hub, a speculative CSCL prototype combining tangible LEGO models with augmented reality. Through workshops with 17 families, researchers found that collaborative learning emerges via material interaction and shared problem-solving, with family roles dynamically shifting. Rather than traditional adult-to-child knowledge transfer, findings reveal multidirectional zones of proximal development where children, parents, and digital artifacts alternately serve as "more knowledgeable others," enabling intergenerational co-construction of understanding about datafication and algorithmic systems.
